Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Everyone points or moves at once. Ask one or two people from different corners why, if they want to say. Across 73 studies, moving toward a commitment that fits was about twice as common as sliding back. A 650-word college essay doesn’t change that.

Slide 3 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 4 · Notes

Erikson called figuring out who you are the central task of adolescence. Marcia boiled it to two questions: have you explored, have you committed? You can be in a different box for each part of you: settled on music, trying things on with faith, haven’t thought about politics. A commitment you chose after looking around can look exactly like one you were handed. The difference is that it’s yours.

Slide 5 · Notes

Three quiet minutes. Often it’s the piece other people notice most, or the one you’re questioning. Across 46 studies, minority youth who felt good about their racial or ethnic group had fewer symptoms of depression and better self-esteem (Rivas-Drake et al., 2014). White students in mostly white places may not think about this until later, and everyone has a cultural story. Mixed, adopted, or the child of immigrants: you may be building a few at once.

Slide 6 · Notes

After the vote, the answer. About 19,000 adults ages 18 to 68 (Quoidbach, Gilbert & Wilson, 2013). It compared people of different ages, so it’s a rough picture, and the pattern was clear.

Slide 7 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 8 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody has to share their own label.

Slide 9 · Notes

Take a few. Then three moments, one at a time.

Slide 10 · Notes

Talk it through as a circle. Keeping it to herself or “it’s my life” both close the door. The best answer keeps the family in it.

Slide 11 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 12 · Notes

All of these are fine, including “Why do you ask? I get that a lot.”

Slide 13 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 14 · Notes

Telling other friends isn’t Sam’s call to make, and “it’s probably a phase” shuts the friend down. Keep the talk on Sam’s response, never on guessing anyone’s identity.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

Private, on the index card. Other options from the student page: name three values you can steer by, follow something new, or find one place to be all of you. Interviewing your roots doesn’t assume who’s at home.

Slide 17 · Notes

If a student comes out in the circle, thank them simply and check in afterward. Harassment, being outed, or feeling you have to hide who you are everywhere goes to a counselor that day.

Slide 18 · Notes

Share the take-home link (post it on your advisory page too). It has the four places to be, a private check-in, and who to talk to, including the Trevor Project and 988.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can describe identity as exploring and then committing, know that it keeps developing through the 20s, and choose one low-stakes way to explore or one place to be all of themselves. Nobody has to share anything about their own identity.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Four corners of the room: agree, disagree, not sure, it depends
  • Index cards for the private reflection and the closing experiment
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minFour corners: know who you are by graduation?
  2. 3 minFour places to be
  3. 3 minWhich piece of you feels biggest (private)
  4. 2 minFour corners: do adults expect to change?
  5. 3 minLabels: turn and talk, share out
  6. 4 minThree moments: Ellie, Gabe, Sam
  7. 2 minOne experiment, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Four corners on graduation, the four places to be, the pieces of you (private), and one experiment.

Before you teach
Nobody shares their own identity.

Gender, sexuality, faith, immigration, adoption and money can be private, or unsafe to talk about. Every share today is optional. Never ask a student to speak for their whole group, and don't turn to the one student in the circle who shares a background.

Four corners is about the research statements.

Students vote on what the research says, never on anything personal. Pointing works as well as walking, and "it depends" is always a fine corner.

If a student comes out in the circle.

Thank them simply ("Thanks for telling us"), keep going, and don't make it a moment. Check in privately afterward. Remind the group at the start that what people say in advisory stays in advisory, while being honest that you'd get help if someone's safety were at risk.

Harassment and outing go to a counselor that day.

If a student is being harassed or threatened because of their race, religion, gender, sexuality or disability, or someone outed them or is sharing private photos, that is a same-day counselor conversation, not a discussion topic.

Keep families in the story.

The Ellie scenario is about a family plan. Families pass down a lot worth keeping: language, faith, food, values, stories. Building your own identity can include choosing much of what you were given. Don't let the discussion turn into teens against families.

Know when it's more than figuring things out.

Feeling you have to hide who you are everywhere, including at home, or thoughts of hurting yourself, go to a counselor the same day. Don't ask about these in advisory. Students can call or text 988 any time. The Trevor Project (1-866-488-7386, or text START to 678-678) is there for LGBTQ+ young people, and Trans Lifeline is at 877-565-8860.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Everyone has a racial and cultural story.

Students of color often start thinking about racial identity early because the world brings it up. White students in mostly white places may not until later. The "where are you really from" scenario lets students practice without anyone in the circle having to tell their own story.

Gender and sexuality: their timeline, their words.

Some students know early, some question for a while, some land where they started. All of it is identity work. Nobody owes anyone a label, and who to tell, and when, is the student's call, with safety first. A student who isn't out at home needs a school adult route: a counselor can help them figure out who to talk to.

"Interview your roots" doesn't assume who's at home.

Students live with one parent, two moms or two dads, grandparents, foster or kinship families, or between two homes. Adopted students may not have access to some of their story. Any elder, family friend, coach or mentor who knows part of their story counts.

Faith can be kept, questioned, or chosen.

For some students faith is the steadiest piece. Others are questioning it, or grew up without one. Keeping a faith after thinking it through is as much a commitment that fits as anything else. Don't present questioning as the goal.

Body and ability is one of the pieces.

For disabled and chronically ill students, disability can be a source of pride and community, not only something other people notice. Include it in the list without making it the example of something hard.

Language and code switching.

Children of immigrants and students whose home language isn't English may switch how they talk, dress or act between home and school. It is a real skill, and it can be tiring when you never get a break. Mixed students don't have to pick a side.

What the research says

Psychologist Erik Erikson called building a sense of who you are and where you fit the central task of adolescence.

Erikson, Identity: Youth and Crisis, 1968

Identity can be described by two questions: Have you explored your options? Have you committed to something? The answers make four common places to be, and a person can be in a different place for each part of themselves.

Marcia, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1966

Across 73 studies, the most common change from the teens into the 20s was from exploring to a commitment that fits. Moving forward was about twice as common as sliding back.

Kroger, Martinussen and Marcia, Journal of Adolescence, 2010

Across 46 studies, minority youth who felt good about their ethnic or racial group had fewer symptoms of depression, better self-esteem, fewer problems with drugs and alcohol, and did better in school.

Rivas-Drake et al., Child Development, 2014

Ethnic and racial identity develops across adolescence and into young adulthood. Students of color often start this work early; white students in mostly white settings may start later.

Umaña-Taylor et al., Child Development, 2014

People start building a life story about where they came from and where they're headed in adolescence. People who find growth or meaning in a hard stretch tend to do better than those who tell it as a dead end.

McAdams and McLean, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2013

In a study of about 19,000 adults ages 18 to 68, people at every age said they'd changed a lot in the past ten years and expected to change very little in the next ten: the "end of history illusion." It compared people of different ages, so it's a rough picture.

Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson, Science, 2013
